variants.prompt: Why does sharding parameters in FSDP not split a forward pass into separate model stages?
variants.answer: Each rank gathers the parameters it needs and executes the full model on its own examples. Parameter storage is sharded, not the sequence of layer computations.
variants.explanation: Parameter ownership and computation ownership are different choices. FSDP temporarily reconstructs each needed layer on every rank, so it remains data parallel despite distributing stored weights; pipeline parallelism instead assigns different layers to different devices.

variants.prompt: An FSDP rank executes all model layers on its local examples.
variants.explanation: Each rank advances its own examples through the complete model, gathering missing weights when needed. The stored parameter shard is not a permanent restriction on which layers it can execute, which distinguishes FSDP from dividing model stages across ranks.

variants.prompt: Why can the critical batch size limit useful data-parallel scaling?
variants.answer: Each device needs its own examples ($M<B$), so adding devices means growing the batch $B$. Once $B$ would pass the critical batch size, more data-parallel devices stop being worth it.
variants.explanation: Data parallelism gives each of the $M$ devices its own slice of the batch, so the device count is tied to $B$. A batch larger than the critical batch size is undesirable, so data parallelism runs out of devices it can usefully feed. Model parallelism breaks the tie by splitting the computation of one forward pass instead of the batch.

variants.prompt: Data parallelism needs the batch to hold more examples than there are devices.
variants.explanation: Data parallelism splits the examples of a batch over the $M$ devices, so it requires $M<B$: a device without an example has nothing to compute. That ties the device count to $B$, and $B$ should stay below the critical batch size, which caps how far data parallelism alone can scale. Model parallelism avoids the cap by splitting one forward pass.

variants.prompt: ZeRO-3 parameter sharding also divides activation tensors across the same ranks.
variants.explanation: ZeRO-3 shards parameters, gradients and optimizer states and gathers each layer’s weights just in time, but every rank still runs the full forward pass on its own examples and stores their activations. Weight memory and activation memory are separate limits, so sharding model state cannot fix the second; splitting the sequence length across devices (sequence parallelism) targets it.

variants.prompt: Why can sequence parallelism reduce per-rank activation memory even after ZeRO-3 has sharded the model state?
variants.answer: It distributes activations along the token dimension. ZeRO-3 shards parameters, gradients and optimizer state, but does not itself partition the local activation tensors.
variants.explanation: Persistent model state and activations are separate memory costs. Sharding the sequence dimension gives each rank a smaller portion of the token activations; further parameter sharding cannot remove an activation-memory bottleneck. This is why the two approaches can address different limits.

variants.prompt: Which assignment lets devices cooperate inside one weight-matrix multiplication?
variants.explanation: Tensor parallelism partitions work inside a layer; pipeline parallelism assigns successive stages, and data parallelism assigns different examples. Expert placement distributes MoE experts rather than necessarily dividing a matrix. ⚠️ Note: the introductory 5D list swaps the TP and PP descriptions and labels pipeline parallelism as TP.

variants.prompt: How does expert parallelism divide a mixture-of-experts model?
variants.answer: It assigns different experts to different devices.
variants.explanation: The partition follows expert identity, giving a different axis from dividing examples, sequence positions, or pieces of a weight matrix. This is why expert parallelism can be listed separately from data, sequence, and tensor parallelism in the same multidimensional arrangement.

variants.prompt: With expert parallelism alone, what is the smallest piece of an MoE layer that one GPU must hold in full?
variants.answer: A whole expert. Expert parallelism assigns entire experts to devices and never splits one expert’s weights, so each expert must fit on its GPU; splitting an expert needs another axis such as tensor parallelism.
variants.explanation: Expert parallelism partitions an MoE layer by expert identity: different experts live on different devices, which spreads the total expert memory. It does nothing inside an expert, whose weight matrices stay whole. Tensor parallelism is the axis that splits individual weight matrices, so the two are combined when a single expert is too large for one device.

variants.prompt: Which parallelism axis scales throughput rather than cutting the model or activation memory each device holds?
variants.explanation: Data parallelism replicates the model and gives each device different examples, so it adds throughput without shrinking per-device model memory. Tensor and pipeline parallelism split the model (weight matrices, or groups of layers) to cut model memory, and sequence parallelism splits the token dimension to cut activation memory. ⚠️ Note: the intro’s 5D list swaps the TP and PP definitions (and labels PP “TP”); the TP and PP sections confirm that TP splits weight matrices and PP places layers on different devices.

variants.prompt: Pipeline parallelism, like tensor parallelism, is mainly a way to fit the model in memory rather than to raise throughput.
variants.explanation: Both split the model itself, PP by placing groups of layers on different devices and TP by splitting weight matrices, so each device stores only part of the weights. Naive layer placement does not even raise throughput; micro-batching only recovers the idle time it creates. Scaling throughput is data parallelism’s job, and activation memory is sequence parallelism’s.

variants.prompt: Perfect strong scaling keeps each chip’s FLOPs per second constant as chips are added.
variants.explanation: Strong scaling means that training throughput (FLOPs/second) grows in proportion to the number of chips. If $M$ chips give $M$ times the throughput of one, each chip still delivers what it did alone, so the per-chip rate is unchanged. Anything that makes chips wait, such as communication or pipeline idle time, lowers the per-chip rate and breaks the proportionality.

variants.prompt: One rank owns initialized weights; every other rank needs an identical copy. Which collective fits?
variants.explanation: Broadcast starts from one owner and distributes that owner’s data. All-gather instead assembles distinct pieces initially held by multiple ranks; the two reduction operations combine contributions numerically, which is unnecessary when there is already one authoritative value.

variants.prompt: Why is all-gather needed instead of broadcast when every rank owns a different parameter shard?
variants.answer: Every rank contributes a different piece that must be assembled; broadcasting a single rank’s shard cannot reconstruct the whole tensor.
variants.explanation: A broadcast duplicates one source, while an all-gather concatenates the distributed pieces into a full collection on each participant. FSDP uses the latter because parameter ownership is spread across ranks, even though computation temporarily needs the complete layer.

variants.prompt: What happens to $\mathbf A[I,J_Y]$ after an all-gather over $Y$?
variants.answer: It becomes $\mathbf A[I,J]$, replicated over $Y$.
variants.explanation: The transformation is $\operatorname{AllGather}_Y:\mathbf A[I,J_Y]\rightarrow\mathbf A[I,J]$. Each rank receives the missing column shards, so the $Y$ subscript disappears; unlike reduction, this operation does not sum overlapping contributions.

variants.prompt: All-gather sums the corresponding elements contributed by different ranks.
variants.explanation: All-gather preserves the separate pieces and assembles them into a complete tensor on each rank. Summing contributions belongs to reduce-scatter or all-reduce; confusing these operations would turn parameter reconstruction into a numerically different operation.

variants.prompt: With sharded optimizer state, how should local gradients be combined and delivered to parameter owners?
variants.explanation: Reduce-scatter combines the contributions and distributes distinct pieces of the result. All-reduce would leave the entire reduced vector on every rank, while all-gather and broadcast do not perform the required summation; this distinction enables sharded optimizer ownership.

variants.prompt: Why does ordinary DDP use all-reduce rather than reduce-scatter for gradients?
variants.answer: Every rank updates the complete parameter vector, so each rank needs the complete aggregated gradient.
variants.explanation: All-reduce combines local contributions and makes the final vector available on every rank. Reduce-scatter would leave only a subset, sufficient for a sharded optimizer but insufficient for DDP’s identical full-vector updates; the required output layout determines the collective.

variants.prompt: After the gradient sync in plain DDP, each rank holds only its own shard of the averaged gradient.
variants.explanation: A sharded result is what reduce-scatter gives, and ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 rely on it. Plain DDP all-reduces, so every rank ends with the complete averaged gradient, because every rank then updates all the parameters with its own full copy of the optimizer state.

variants.prompt: Why can ring all-reduce be split into reduce-scatter followed by all-gather?
variants.answer: The first phase computes the final reduced shards; the second replicates those shards so every rank gets the complete result.
variants.explanation: A rank does not need the whole answer while reduction is in progress: it can finish the sum for one shard. Once each shard has an owner with its final value, all-gather distributes those values without further summation. This separation is what allows ZeRO-1 to insert shard-local parameter updates between the two collectives.

variants.prompt: In ring all-reduce, the all-gather phase does the additions while reduce-scatter only moves data.
variants.explanation: It is the reverse: reduce-scatter does all the arithmetic and leaves each GPU with one fully reduced chunk, then all-gather does pure copying so every GPU receives every reduced chunk. Neither phase repeats the other’s work, which is why the pair costs the same as one all-reduce and why ZeRO-1 can slot a sharded update between them.

variants.prompt: Which part of ring all-reduce performs the summation, and what remains for the other part?
variants.answer: Reduce-scatter performs the summation; all-gather distributes the already reduced shards.
variants.explanation: The final values of individual shards are established before all-gather starts. The second phase copies those values instead of summing them again, explaining why replacing all-reduce with its two constituent phases can accommodate sharded updates.

variants.prompt: The all-gather phase of ring all-reduce distributes values that are already reduced.
variants.explanation: Reduction has completed for each shard during reduce-scatter, although no single rank yet has every shard. All-gather removes that remaining distribution by copying the reduced pieces; another summation at this point would change their values.

variants.prompt: How can ring all-reduce combine every rank’s data without direct communication between every pair of ranks?
variants.answer: Ranks forward and reduce chunks through neighboring ranks; contributions propagate around the ring over multiple steps.
variants.explanation: Global participation does not require a direct link for each pair of participants. Each rank sends toward one neighbor and receives from another, allowing chunks to accumulate contributions as they travel. The ring topology therefore describes local exchanges, while the collective result still includes all ranks.

variants.prompt: An all-reduce of a fixed-size array takes 10 ms on 8 GPUs. At the same per-GPU bandwidth, how long does it take on 64 GPUs?
variants.explanation: For all-gather, reduce-scatter and all-reduce, communication time depends only on the array size and the bandwidth, not on how many devices the array is sharded over, so it stays at about 10 ms. The tempting 80 ms assumes cost grows with the number of participants. (General context, not from the notes: in a ring, each GPU sends about $\frac{M-1}{M}$ of the array per phase, a fraction that barely changes with $M$; per-step latency is ignored.)

variants.prompt: Running the same all-gather over twice as many GPUs leaves its communication time roughly unchanged.
variants.explanation: The time of all-gather, reduce-scatter and all-reduce is set by the array size over the bandwidth; the device count drops out. Each GPU’s own shard shrinks as devices are added, but it still has to receive the rest of the array, so the bytes per GPU stay close to the full array size. (General context, not from the notes: this ignores the per-step latency, which does grow with the ring length.)

variants.prompt: Why is the backward of all-gather a reduce-scatter?
variants.answer: A source shard was used on multiple ranks, so its gradient contributions must be summed and returned to the rank that owns it.
variants.explanation: Forward replication creates multiple uses of the same source value, and their backward contributions accumulate at that source. Returning only the owner’s slice also restores the original sharding. ⚠️ Note: the source chain-rule example duplicates a derivative term and incorrectly writes the branching relation; the fan-out/sum principle is the sound part.

variants.prompt: Which collective accumulates gradients back to the original shard owners after a forward all-gather?
variants.explanation: The replicated downstream uses each contribute a gradient, so backward must sum their contributions and retain only the original owner’s slice. Broadcast and all-gather copy without that sum; all-reduce supplies the sum but leaves a full replicated tensor instead of the original sharding.

variants.prompt: Why is the backward of a sum reduce-scatter an all-gather, rather than another reduction?
variants.answer: Each summed input receives the gradient of its output chunk; those chunk gradients must be gathered back to all contributing ranks.
variants.explanation: For a summation, each contributing input has derivative one, so the output gradient is copied to every contributor. Gathering the different output chunks restores the input layout; applying another reduce-scatter would instead sum and shard the wrong quantities.

variants.prompt: Backward through a sum reduce-scatter divides each output-chunk gradient by the number of contributing ranks.
variants.explanation: A sum sends the same upstream gradient to each summand; it does not divide that gradient by the number of contributors. Gathering all output chunks delivers those gradients to the original inputs, mirroring the all-gather/reduce-scatter pairing in the reverse direction.

variants.prompt: In the forward pass, every rank sums its tensor with the other ranks’ and keeps the full sum. Which collective does the backward pass need?
variants.explanation: Every rank’s output depends on every rank’s input, so each input’s gradient is the sum of the upstream gradients of all ranks, needed on every rank: another all-reduce. Equivalently, all-reduce is reduce-scatter then all-gather, and backward reverses the order and swaps each for its partner, giving reduce-scatter then all-gather again. All-gather alone would copy without summing, and reduce-scatter would leave each rank only a shard.

variants.prompt: Using the two phases of ring all-reduce, derive what the backward pass of an all-reduce is.
variants.answer: All-reduce is reduce-scatter then all-gather. Backward runs them in reverse, each replaced by its partner: the all-gather’s backward is a reduce-scatter, then the reduce-scatter’s backward is an all-gather. So the backward is again an all-reduce.
variants.explanation: An all-gather fans each shard out to every device, so its backward sums the gradients back onto the owner (reduce-scatter); a reduce-scatter sums many inputs into one chunk, so its backward copies the chunk’s gradient to every contributor (all-gather). Reversing reduce-scatter then all-gather therefore gives reduce-scatter then all-gather: fan-out becomes a sum and a sum becomes a fan-out.

variants.prompt: If $Y$ is absent from $\mathbf A[I_X,J]$, how does the tensor vary across mesh axis $Y$?
variants.answer: It is replicated across $Y$; only the $I$ dimension is partitioned, along $X$.
variants.explanation: A mesh axis appearing as a tensor-axis subscript indicates partitioning over that mesh axis. An absent mesh axis indicates replication, not a missing tensor dimension; this lets one matrix be sharded on one mesh axis while serving as the repeated operand along another.

variants.prompt: $\mathbf A[I_{XY},J]$ partitions rows across the flattened $XY$ mesh.
variants.explanation: The subscript $XY$ assigns the row dimension $I$ across both mesh axes, rather than only along $X$ or $Y$. By contrast, an axis absent from the tensor’s partition specification carries replicas; the notation describes placement, not a change to the mathematical matrix.

variants.prompt: When can a distributed matrix multiplication compute its output blocks without communicating between ranks?
variants.answer: When each rank has the full contracting dimension for its assigned output rows and columns; only the non-contracting dimensions are sharded.
variants.explanation: Every output element sums over the contracting dimension. If that dimension is complete locally, the rank has every term for its output block, even when other ranks own other rows or columns. Column-parallel linear layers are this case: each device computes a complete slice of the output. Splitting the contraction instead produces incomplete sums that must be combined.

variants.prompt: How many collective operations does $\mathbf A[I_X,J]\cdot\mathbf B[J,K_Y]\rightarrow\mathbf C[I_X,K_Y]$ need?
variants.explanation: The contracting dimension $J$ is unsharded, so the device at mesh position $(x,y)$ holds full rows of $\mathbf A$ (block $I_x$) and full columns of $\mathbf B$ (block $K_y$), and computes its block of $\mathbf C$ locally, already sharded as $[I_X,K_Y]$. Communication is only needed when $J$ is sharded: an all-gather if one operand is, an all-reduce of partial sums if both are.

variants.prompt: For a matrix product with only one operand sharded along the contraction, what communication before multiplication makes each local result complete?
variants.answer: All-gather the sharded operand so each rank has its full contraction dimension, matching the replicated operand.
variants.explanation: The gather restores the missing input blocks before multiplication, so every local product includes the whole contraction. When both operands instead have matching contraction shards, ranks can multiply locally first and reduce the partial products afterward. The distinction is where the missing sum is completed.

variants.prompt: In $\mathbf A[I,J_X]\cdot\mathbf B[J_X,K]$, what does each device hold after its local matmul, and what completes the product?
variants.answer: A full-shape $[I,K]$ partial sum over its slice of $J$, written $\mathbf C[I,K]\{U_X\}$. An all-reduce over $X$ adds the partial sums and gives every device the complete product.
variants.explanation: The full product is the sum of the local products, $\mathbf C=\sum_x\mathbf A[I,J_x]\mathbf B[J_x,K]$. An all-reduce completes and replicates it, whereas an all-gather would concatenate overlapping partial results without adding them. The row-parallel down projection of a tensor-parallel MLP is this case: $y=h_0W2_0+h_1W2_1$.

variants.prompt: When both matmul operands are sharded along the contracting dimension, each device’s local product already has the full output shape.
variants.explanation: Each device multiplies $\mathbf A[I,J_x]$ by $\mathbf B[J_x,K]$, a full $I\times K$ result, but it sums only over its slice of $J$. The shape is complete while the values are partial, $\mathbf C[I,K]\{U_X\}$, so an all-reduce over $X$ must add them; concatenating would be wrong. Output shape alone does not tell you whether a distributed matmul is finished.

variants.prompt: DDP ranks see different examples. Why do their parameter replicas remain synchronized?
variants.answer: They aggregate and average gradients before applying the same optimizer update to the same starting parameters and optimizer states.
variants.explanation: Local gradients differ because local examples differ, but all-reduce gives every rank the same combined gradient. Each rank then repeats the full update independently; exchanging parameters is unnecessary in this idealized loop because equal inputs to the update yield equal replicas.

variants.prompt: In ordinary DDP, each rank updates the complete parameter vector after gradient synchronization.
variants.explanation: The model and optimizer state are replicated, so each rank can apply the same full-vector update after receiving the averaged gradients. ZeRO-1 changes this ownership pattern by letting each rank update only its own subset and then gathering the updated parameters.

variants.prompt: In the simplified DDP training loop, what is exchanged between ranks?
variants.explanation: Each rank holds the full model, so its forward pass needs nothing from other ranks; the only exchange is the gradient all-reduce, which happens during backward. Per-layer weight gathering is FSDP’s extra cost, activation hand-offs between devices belong to pipeline parallelism, and gathering updated parameters after the step is what ZeRO-1 adds.

variants.prompt: Why does the simplified DDP forward pass need no per-layer parameter all-gather?
variants.answer: Every rank already holds the entire parameter vector.
variants.explanation: DDP replicates weights and computes all layers locally on its assigned examples. Only the separately computed gradient contributions need to be reconciled for the update; FSDP saves weight storage by changing this assumption and gathering missing layer parameters when required.

variants.prompt: What redundant state and work does ZeRO-1 remove from each DDP rank?
variants.answer: It shards optimizer state, so each rank stores the state and performs updates for only its assigned parameters.
variants.explanation: DDP duplicates the optimizer state and the complete update on every rank. ZeRO-1 distributes that ownership while leaving the model usable as a full replica for local computation; reduced gradient slices go to their owners, and updated parameter slices are gathered afterward.

variants.prompt: Going from plain DDP to ZeRO stage 1, which per-device memory shrinks?
variants.explanation: ZeRO-1 gives each of the $M$ devices $1/M$ of the Adam vectors and lets it update only the matching parameters. Full gradients are still computed and held until the reduce-scatter (sharding them is ZeRO-2), parameters stay replicated (sharding them is ZeRO-3), and no ZeRO stage splits activations.

variants.prompt: Which sequence implements the ZeRO-1 update after local gradients are computed?
variants.explanation: Reduce-scatter leaves each rank the summed gradient for exactly the parameters whose Adam state it owns; it updates those, then all-gather rebuilds the full updated parameters everywhere. All-reduce then a full update is plain DDP; ending with an all-reduce would sum parameter shards instead of concatenating them; gathering first would spread unsummed gradients.

variants.prompt: How does ZeRO-1’s communication per training step compare with plain DDP’s, and why?
variants.answer: It is the same. DDP’s gradient all-reduce costs as much as a reduce-scatter plus an all-gather, which is exactly what ZeRO-1 does: reduce-scatter the gradients, update the owned shard, all-gather the updated parameters.
variants.explanation: Ring all-reduce is itself reduce-scatter followed by all-gather, so ZeRO-1 only slots the shard-local optimizer step between the two phases and gathers parameters instead of gradients, arrays of the same size. That makes its $1/M$ optimizer-state memory a free win. ZeRO-2 keeps the same collectives and changes only when gradients are reduce-scattered and freed.

variants.prompt: ZeRO-1 pays for its optimizer-memory savings with extra communication compared with DDP.
variants.explanation: One all-reduce costs the same as a reduce-scatter plus an all-gather, and that pair is all ZeRO-1 communicates: gradients are reduce-scattered to their owners, and the updated parameter shards are all-gathered. The savings are free in communication; the price of sharding shows up only at ZeRO-3, which must gather weights before each layer can run.

variants.prompt: What must ZeRO-2 do during backward to avoid retaining the full gradient vector?
variants.answer: Reduce-scatter gradients as they become available, keep the rank’s reduced slice, and free the other portions.
variants.explanation: Sharding only after every gradient has accumulated would miss the intended reduction in retained gradient memory. Layerwise reduction and release change the lifetime of those tensors; parameter replicas remain complete, distinguishing this stage from ZeRO-3.

variants.prompt: ZeRO-2 waits for the entire full gradient vector before freeing unowned layer gradients.
variants.explanation: As layer gradients become available, they are reduce-scattered and the non-owned portions are released. Waiting until all layers finish would retain the very gradient storage this stage aims to remove; ZeRO-1’s optimizer-state partition alone does not accomplish that.

variants.prompt: How does ZeRO-3 execute every model layer on each rank while keeping persistent parameter storage sharded?
choices: Send activations to the rank owning the layer
All-gather a layer’s weights just before use
All-reduce a layer’s weight shards before use
Reduce-scatter a layer’s weights before use
variants.explanation: ZeRO-3 all-gathers a layer’s parameter shards right before the layer runs, uses the full weights, then discards them. An all-reduce would add the shards together instead of concatenating them, and a reduce-scatter would shard them further. Sending activations to the owner of each layer is pipeline-style placement, not data parallelism.

variants.prompt: What does ZeRO-3 add beyond ZeRO-2 to reduce persistent model-state memory?
variants.answer: It shards parameters as well as gradients and optimizer states, gathering layer weights just in time.
variants.explanation: ZeRO-2 still keeps a full parameter replica on every device; ZeRO-3 shards the parameters too and all-gathers each layer’s weights just in time, then discards them. That is what lets it train models that do not fit on one GPU, although the gathered layer and the activations must still fit. ⚠️ Note: this stage writes the per-device share as $1/N$, where the chapter elsewhere uses $M$ for the device count.

variants.prompt: Which ZeRO stage shards gradients and optimizer state but retains complete parameter replicas?
variants.explanation: Stage 1 partitions optimizer state, stage 2 additionally partitions retained gradients, and stage 3 additionally partitions stored parameters. DDP replicates all three classes of state; distinguishing these classes prevents attributing parameter-memory savings to stage 2.

variants.prompt: Why can ZeRO-3 fit a model whose parameters exceed one GPU’s capacity while ZeRO-2 cannot?
variants.answer: ZeRO-3 shards stored parameters; ZeRO-2 still stores the full parameter vector on every rank.
variants.explanation: ZeRO-2 partitions gradients and optimizer state but leaves weight replicas intact. ZeRO-3 removes that persistent weight replication and gathers each needed layer temporarily; enough memory must still remain for that layer and its activations.

variants.prompt: Why does placing successive layers on separate GPUs fail to improve throughput by itself?
variants.answer: A single batch still traverses the layers sequentially, leaving other stages waiting; placement alone does not overlap useful work.
variants.explanation: The next stage cannot start that batch until the previous stage has produced its hidden states. Moving layers solves a placement problem but does not by itself create concurrent stage execution; splitting the batch into micro-batches supplies independent work to overlap.

variants.prompt: With one layer per GPU and an unsplit batch, the GPUs take turns computing rather than working at the same time.
variants.explanation: Layer $\ell+1$ cannot start until layer $\ell$ has produced the hidden states for the whole batch, so at any moment one GPU computes while the others wait. This placement spreads the weights over devices but not the work, hence no throughput gain. Splitting the batch into micro-batches, as `Pipe(model, chunks=8)` does, lets different GPUs work on different micro-batches at once.

variants.prompt: In pipeline parallelism, why does splitting a batch into micro-batches improve device utilization?
variants.answer: Different micro-batches occupy different stages at once, so one stage need not wait while another processes the entire batch.
variants.explanation: A stage can pass the first micro-batch onward and begin the next, while the following stage works on the first. The dependency remains sequential within a micro-batch but no longer serializes all device work for the whole batch. Merely placing layers on separate devices does not create this overlap.

variants.prompt: In the forward product $Y=XW$ with replicated $X$, why does splitting $W$ by output columns yield complete output slices?
variants.answer: Each shard contains all input rows but only some output columns, so it computes those output coordinates over the complete contraction.
variants.explanation: Writing the columns as blocks gives $Y=X[W_0,W_1]=[XW_0,XW_1]$. The pieces concatenate directly because each sums over the full input dimension; row-sharding instead divides that sum and requires a reduction.

variants.prompt: For the forward product $Y=XW$ with replicated $X$, what does splitting $W$ by output columns produce locally?
choices: A partial sum for every output
A complete slice of the output
A slice of the input gradient
variants.explanation: The output columns follow the weight columns: $X[W_0,W_1]=[XW_0,XW_1]$. Each local output slice is complete because the input contraction is not split; a full-output partial sum is the row-parallel case, and gradients are a separate backward computation.

variants.prompt: In an FFN forward pass, why must outputs of a row-parallel down projection be summed rather than concatenated?
variants.answer: The input features are split, so each device computes a contribution to every output coordinate: $y=h_0W2_0+h_1W2_1$.
variants.explanation: The block product is $y=[h_0,h_1][W2_0;W2_1]=h_0W2_0+h_1W2_1=y_0+y_1$. Each local output has the full output shape but only part of its value; concatenation would increase that shape instead of completing the contraction.

variants.prompt: In an FFN forward pass, row-parallel down projections produce full-shaped partial sums that need reduction.
variants.explanation: Each rank multiplies its input-feature shard by the matching weight rows, giving $y_0$ or $y_1$ rather than separate output-coordinate blocks. The complete answer is $y=y_0+y_1$, which is why all-reduce follows the down projection instead of all-gathering its outputs.

variants.prompt: With replicated inputs, which weight-sharding order avoids a collective between the projections of a two-layer, elementwise-activation MLP?
variants.explanation: The first projection leaves complete shards along the expanded feature dimension, allowing the activation to run locally. The second projection consumes those same shards and produces contributions that are summed at the end; reversing the first split would require completing a sum before the activation.

variants.prompt: Why can the activation stay local between column-parallel and row-parallel MLP projections?
variants.answer: Each rank already owns complete values for its subset of intermediate features, and the activation acts elementwise on those features.
variants.explanation: The first projection partitions output coordinates rather than contributions to the same coordinate. Applying the activation therefore does not require information from other ranks, and the second projection is partitioned to accept exactly that feature layout.

variants.prompt: For a nonlinear activation, applying it separately to row-parallel partial sums is equivalent to reducing first.
variants.explanation: In general, $\operatorname{SiLU}(y_0+y_1)\ne\operatorname{SiLU}(y_0)+\operatorname{SiLU}(y_1)$. Row-parallel outputs must be summed before the activation has the intended input; this explains why the communication-saving MLP arrangement starts with column parallelism.

variants.prompt: What forces communication before the activation if the first MLP projection is row-parallel?
variants.answer: The projection outputs are incomplete sums, and a nonlinear activation must see the completed values.
variants.explanation: A row-parallel product leaves contributions to each output rather than complete feature coordinates. Since $\operatorname{SiLU}(y_0+y_1)\ne\operatorname{SiLU}(y_0)+\operatorname{SiLU}(y_1)$ in general, the sum must be completed first; column parallelism avoids this intermediate dependency.

variants.prompt: For one MLP forward pass with replicated input, a column-parallel up projection and row-parallel down projection, how many all-reduces are needed?
variants.explanation: The up projection produces complete feature shards, and the elementwise activation operates locally on them. Only the down projection produces partial sums that must be combined, giving one final all-reduce. This count excludes backward communication and collectives introduced by additional parallelism schemes.

variants.prompt: In a SwiGLU FFN, how must the up and gate projection shards be placed so their elementwise product needs no communication?
variants.answer: Their feature shards along $F$ must align, so each rank holds matching gate and up-projection coordinates.
variants.explanation: The local computation pairs matching coordinates in $\operatorname{Swish}(\mathbf G)\odot\mathbf U$, preserving the $F$ shards for the row-parallel down projection. ⚠️ Note: the source names the gate projection twice; the intended pair is $W_\text{gate}$ and $W_\text{up}$.

variants.prompt: In a SwiGLU FFN, the up and gate projections can use different feature-to-rank assignments without communication before their elementwise product.
variants.explanation: The product $\operatorname{Swish}(\mathbf G)\odot\mathbf U$ pairs each coordinate of the gate with the same coordinate of the up projection, so both must sit on the same rank. Column-sharding $W_\text{gate}$ and $W_\text{up}$ with the same split of $F$ keeps the product local and sharded on $F$, ready for the row-parallel $W_\text{down}$ and the single all-reduce at the end.

variants.prompt: Tensor-parallel attention splits the QKV projection’s output columns across GPUs. How must they be grouped so attention needs no communication, and why?
variants.answer: By head: each GPU gets the full Q, K and V columns of a subset of heads. Heads compute their scores, softmax and weighted values independently, so everything up to the output projection is local.
variants.explanation: Attention mixes positions within a head but never mixes heads, so a rank holding complete heads has all it needs. The QKV projection is column-parallel and the output projection row-parallel, and one all-reduce combines the latter’s partial sums, as in the MLP. The code asserts that the head count is divisible by the world size so that each rank gets whole heads.

variants.prompt: With tensor parallelism on both attention and the MLP, how many all-reduces does one transformer layer’s forward pass need?
variants.explanation: Each block is column-parallel then row-parallel: attention runs QKV column-parallel, per-head attention locally, then a row-parallel output projection; the MLP runs the up projection column-parallel, the activation locally, then a row-parallel down projection. Each row-parallel layer ends in one all-reduce of partial sums, so $1+1=2$ per layer in the forward pass (backward not counted).

variants.prompt: In tensor-parallel attention, the outputs of heads held by different GPUs are first mixed by the output projection’s all-reduce.
variants.explanation: Inside attention each head is self-contained, so no rank needs another rank’s heads. The output projection is row-parallel: each rank multiplies its heads’ outputs by its rows of the projection, giving a full-shape partial sum, and the all-reduce adds those contributions. That sum is the first place where heads from different GPUs meet.

variants.prompt: FSDP is combined with tensor parallelism on an MLP. What does sharding the FFN dimension $F$ reduce?
choices: Activation memory along the sequence axis
Bytes moved by each weight all-gather
variants.explanation: FSDP’s communication is all-gathering weights before use; with $W^\text{up}$ and $W^\text{down}$ also split along $F$, each device only gathers its $F$-shard, so each gather moves less. Sequence activations are sequence parallelism’s target, idle stages a pipeline issue, and the MLP still needs its one all-reduce. ⚠️ Note: the notes also say sharding $B$ shrinks all-gathers without saying which ones (General context, not from the notes: usually the TP activation all-gathers).
